question.text: What is the PRIMARY distinction between a Long-Short Equity Strategy and a Market-Neutral Strategy in Cat III AIFs?

answer.text: Long-short aims to profit from mispricing with net directional exposure allowed; market-neutral aims to eliminate systematic risk (Beta ~ 0).
Long-short uses leverage; market-neutral does not.
Market-neutral holds only bonds; long-short holds only equities.
Long-short is prohibited in Cat III; market-neutral is permitted.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 10.1.1.3, long-short takes advantage of under/over-valued stocks WITH directional exposure (net long in 130/30). Market-neutral deliberately sizes positions so Beta ~ 0, aiming to harvest ONLY the alpha spread, not market direction. The Trap: A is wrong — both can use leverage. C is fabricated. D is wrong — both are permitted. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C covers same. XXI-B has a limited long-short PMS regime. VIII tests Beta math. Manager's Pro-Tip: When onboarding, ask the investor: 'Do you want Beta exposure or pure alpha?' Market-neutral sleeves should be marketed against MIBOR+X, NOT against NIFTY TRI — otherwise your quarterly IR optics look awful in a bull market.
